analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license to buy or own a gun, universal background checks, and bans on assault weapons and silencers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 4 Senate sponsors on December 19, 2022, was referred to the Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or action of any kind before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten federal gun law in one stroke. It would have required anyone buying or owning a gun or ammunition to first get a federal license — including safety training, a background check, and a photo — and raised the minimum purchase age to 21. It would have required background checks on private gun sales, imposed a 7-business-day waiting period, banned semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, banned gun silencers, restricted untraceable "ghost guns," and let families ask a court to temporarily remove guns from someone who poses a danger to themselves or others. It also would have stripped gun manufacturers of their statutory civil liability shield, raised firearms excise taxes, let the Consumer Product Safety Commission set safety standards for guns for the first time, and funded community violence intervention and gun violence research [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people living with the risk of gun violence: households affected by domestic violence and stalking (the bill closes gaps that currently allow some domestic abusers and stalkers to keep guns), communities hit hardest by community violence, students on college campuses, and families who could petition courts to remove guns from someone in crisis. Researchers and community violence intervention organizations would gain dedicated funding [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires a federal license, including safety training and a background check, to buy or possess any firearm or ammunition, and raises the minimum purchase age to 21 [S2][S3].
Closes private-sale loopholes by requiring background checks for transfers between private parties, and imposes a 7-business-day waiting period so checks can be completed [S2][S3].
Bans semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, bans silencers, restricts untraceable 'ghost guns,' and bars multiple-firearm purchases without review [S2][S3].

Lets family members and law enforcement ask a court to remove guns from someone posing a risk of violence (extreme risk protection orders), extends federal protections to dating partners and stalking convictions (closing the 'boyfriend loophole' and 'stalking loophole'), and extends gun-free school zones to colleges [S2][S3].

Requires gun dealers to maintain security plans against theft, repeals the statutory shield that blocks most lawsuits against gun manufacturers, lets the Consumer Product Safety Commission set safety standards for firearms, and raises firearms excise taxes [S2][S3].
Funds community violence intervention programs and federal research on gun violence prevention [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and sellers: the bill bans a product category, raises excise taxes, subjects them to new inspections and liability, and repeals the 2005 law shielding them from most civil lawsuits [S2][S3]. Licensed gun owners bear new licensing, training, and storage requirements, with criminal penalties for unlicensed possession [S3]. Taxpayers fund the licensing system and grant programs [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill would make a federal license — involving safety training with written and live-fire testing, a background investigation, and a photo — a prerequisite for buying or possessing any gun or ammunition, which is a substantially larger barrier to gun ownership than any current federal requirement [S2][S3].
A buyer could not take possession of a gun for at least 7 business days after a background check begins [S3].

The government would gain expanded authority over gun owners: annual background re-investigations of licensees, an ATF petition process to have a court declare an applicant 'unsuitable,' and criminal penalties for unlicensed possession [S3].

Gun makers would lose statutory civil liability protections and could be sued in ways they currently cannot be, and the industry would face higher excise taxes, expanded dealer inspections, and new security-plan requirements [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health case for the bill is substantial: it combines the measures with the strongest research support — licensing, universal background checks, waiting periods, extreme risk protection orders — with new research funding and community intervention grants, and it does not ban hunting rifles or take guns from current lawful owners (existing owners are grandfathered from the licensing requirement [S3]). The costs are real, though: the licensing scheme is a genuine expansion of government oversight into gun ownership, raising legitimate civil-liberties and administrative-burden objections (training, testing, annual checks, possible court denial on "suitability" grounds), and critics argue it primarily burdens law-abiding buyers rather than people who obtain guns illegally. On the other side of the ledger, repealing the industry's civil liability shield and raising excise taxes would finally put part of the public cost of gun violence on the industry rather than entirely on victims and public budgets. Had it passed, the balance would have favored ordinary people by any honest reading of the evidence; instead it never received even a committee hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 19, 2022, during the final two weeks of the 117th Congress, and referred to the Finance Committee, where it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote [S1][S5].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on December 19, 2022, and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Finance [S5].
No further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee report, no floor vote — appears in the action history before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
It attracted only 3 cosponsors, all Senate Democrats, and no Republican support [S4].

The bill is a comprehensive package that touches nearly every part of federal gun law: licensing, background checks, waiting periods, assault weapons, silencers, ghost guns, dealer security, industry liability, consumer safety standards, and research funding [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and sellers, whose current lack of federal licensing, waiting-period, and civil-liability requirements remains untouched. No one in the general public is better off, since the bill would have reduced suicide and homicide risk had it passed. Nobody has an incentive to revive it: had it become law, gun makers would have faced a product ban, higher taxes, and a removal of their civil liability shield.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 19, 2022, the final two weeks of the Congress.

for.name: Sens. Markey, Booker, and Menendez
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsors; no Republican cosponsored.

against.name: Senate Republicans (50 senators)
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and with 50 seats they were positioned to filibuster any floor consideration; the bill never reached the floor.

against.name: National Rifle Association and gun industry groups
against.what_they_did: Long-standing opposition to federal licensing, assault weapon bans, and repeal of the gun industry's civil liability shield, the provisions at the core of this bill.

against.name: Finance Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 19, 2022, and took no action — no hearing or markup — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 4 Senate sponsors and all 3 cosponsors were Democrats or allied independents; no Republican supported it, so the bill sat entirely on one side of the aisle [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill would ban a major product line (semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, plus silencers), raise excise taxes on firearms, and repeal the 2005 statutory shield that protects gun makers from most civil lawsuits, exposing them to litigation [S2][S3].

Dealers would face licensing of their customers, security-plan certification, expanded inspections, employee background checks, and lost-and-stolen reporting requirements, raising compliance costs [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Unlicensed private sellers and ghost gun kit makers
industries.note: Private sales would have to run through a licensed dealer with a background check, and untraceable unserialized guns would be restricted, ending the channels that currently evade background checks [S2][S3].
